description: Hi, I am Richard. I am passionate with data science! Join Me!
summary: We developed Earth Information Jukebox, a browser app that turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into live, real-time sound. Instead of mapping colors directly to notes, it reads each visualization's own colorbar backwards: every pixel's color is converted back into the value it represents, such as ocean temperature or change in night lights, and that value drives the music. The colorbar itself plays as a quiet woodwind octave, a constant pitch reference, while the data moves inside it as a single instrument: a cello for flowing ocean currents (SVS 3912) and a harp for night lights 2012–2023 (SVS 5313). Notes fall on consonant chord tones, so the result stays scientifically faithful and pleasant to hear. This answers the challenge by pairing EIC frames with dynamic sonification generated in real time. It matters because Earth science is still presented almost only visually. With an audio legend, full keyboard control and screen-reader readouts, blind and low-vision people can explore our changing planet, and sighted visitors gain a new way to notice its patterns.
details:
Earth Information Jukebox lets anyone hear NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations, and it is built first for blind and low-vision visitors. It runs live in the browser: pick a visualization and a scan line moves across the animated map while the sound is generated in real time from the pixels on screen. Nothing is pre-recorded.

HOW IT WORKS

EIC visualizations are rendered images, but each one ships with a colorbar. We read that colorbar backwards. Each pixel's hue is matched against a lookup table extracted from the SVS colorbar image, which recovers the physical value the color encodes, and that value is what we sonify.

- The colorbar becomes sound: its two ends are an octave, held quietly in the background by woodwinds. It is a constant pitch reference, the same way the colorbar always stays on screen.

- The data is one instrument moving inside that octave:

• Sea Surface Temperature & Currents (SVS 3912): a bowed cello, whose legato suits flowing currents. Pitch = mean ocean temperature of the scanned row. The scan runs north → south, or west → east inside a fixed latitude band (tropics, 30–60°N, 30–60°S). Notes land on dominant-seventh chord tones, so the data never clashes with the reference, and each sweep becomes an arpeggio that rises toward the warm equator. Land falls silent.

• Night Lights 2012–2023 (SVS 5313): a harp. In the change map it plucks the high D where new lights appeared and the low D where lights went out. In the yearly maps, city lights pluck chord tones, and brighter cities ring higher. The app detects the animation's phase by itself.

ACCESSIBILITY

Fully keyboard operable. An audio legend plays the colorbar as sound before listening. An arrow-key probe plays the value under it and writes its location and value to a screen-reader live region. A one-key text description summarizes the frame (global mean, latitude bands, share of new vs lost lights).

IMPACT

EIC's visual stories reach people who cannot see them, and sighted visitors get a second channel that turns patterns, such as the

warm tropical belt or growth vs loss of lights, i

TOOLS

HTML/JavaScript, Web Audio API (additive synthesib), Python (Pillow, NumPy), ffmpeg, Playwright.

NASA data: SVS 3912, SVS 5313 (EIC content gallery).
